questions.q: What is a hash, in the simplest terms?
options: A digital fingerprint — a fixed-length string generated from any input data
A type of cryptocurrency wallet
The name for a block's position number in the chain
A password chosen by the user
questions.explain: A hash function takes any input (a sentence, a file, a transaction) and turns it into a fixed-length string of numbers and letters.

questions.q: What happens to a hash if you change just one character of the input, like removing a period?
options: The entire hash output changes completely, with nothing in common with the original
Only the last few characters of the hash change
Nothing changes — hashes ignore punctuation
The hash becomes shorter
questions.explain: The live demo showed exactly this: even a tiny change like removing a period produces a totally different hash, with no resemblance to the original.

options: The first block in a blockchain — block number one
The most recent block added to the chain
A special block that stores only failed transactions
The block that contains the most transactions
questions.explain: There's nothing more complicated to it than that — it's simply the first block, the only one that can exist without a predecessor.

questions.q: What does "nonce" stand for, and why does it matter?
options: "Number only used once" — it's the value miners search for during proof-of-work mining
"Network on-chain execution" — a type of smart contract
"New online currency exchange" — a trading platform
It's not a real term used in blockchain
questions.explain: Nonce comes up again when the course covers mining and proof of work — it's literally a number used only once, which miners search for to solve a block.

questions.q: Why does hashing make a blockchain tamper-resistant?
options: Every block includes the hash of the block before it, so changing an old block breaks the link to every block after it
Hashes can be easily reversed to recover the original data
Hashing has nothing to do with blockchain security
Only the genesis block is protected by hashing
questions.explain: Because each block links to the previous block's hash, altering historical data breaks that chain of links in a way that's immediately visible across every copy of the ledger.
